CA-Q001: A cell is one addressable intersection of a row and a column, such as B2. A row or column contains many cells; neither is one cell. A collection of worksheets belongs to the workbook level. Identify the organisational level before deciding where a value or formula is stored.
CA-Q002: A workbook is the file-level container that can hold worksheets; a worksheet supplies a grid of cells. A folder can contain workbook files, but that does not reverse the worksheet/workbook relationship. A formula is an expression entered in a cell, not another name for either container.
CA-Q003: Escape cancels the edit currently in progress, preserving the previously accepted cell contents. Enter normally accepts the edit instead. Cancelling one edit is not the same as undoing every change since opening the workbook, and it does not accept an edit and then clear the cell. Check the formula bar after cancelling.
CA-Q004: The leading apostrophe marks 0017 as text, preserving its identifier representation rather than treating it as the quantity seventeen. The apostrophe is not part of the displayed identifier. The arithmetic alternatives either calculate a number or fail to state a text entry. Ask whether digits identify a record or represent a quantity before calculating with them.
CA-Q005: Separate numeric quantity and price cells allow a formula such as =B2*C2 to calculate the cost and update when an input changes. Combined descriptive text does not provide those two numeric inputs. Words such as four, twelve or pending describe data but do not supply the intended numeric measurements. Keep units in headings and inspect stored values.
CA-Q006: Clear Contents removes the value or formula while leaving its cell and formatting in place. Deleting a cell or an entire row can move surrounding entries and disrupt related fields. A space is still a text entry, so it does not reliably represent an empty cell. Choose the action according to what must remain in the grid.
CA-Q007: AutoComplete suggests an existing text entry in the same column as its opening characters are typed. Extending a numeric series and adjusting copied formulas are fill operations, not that typing aid. Copying formatting changes appearance. Distinguish the mechanism being used even if the same label could also be copied with AutoFill.
CA-Q008: The fill handle can copy selected entries, extend an identified series or propagate formulas into adjacent cells. Its result depends on the selection and fill choice, so one seed value does not always communicate a desired pattern. Number formatting, text suggestions during typing and naming cells are different operations. Inspect the target range before filling.
CA-Q009: Ctrl+D is the source-described Fill Down shortcut, using the upper entry for the selected destination below it. Ctrl+R fills right, Ctrl+Z undoes an action and Ctrl+V pastes clipboard contents. Direction and selection matter: a correct shortcut can still overwrite unintended cells. Its target Microsoft Office keyboard acceptance remains unexecuted here.
CA-Q010: The two selected seeds establish an arithmetic step of 4−2=2. Adding that step gives 6 and then 8. Doubling would instead produce 8 and 16 and represents a different pattern. A repeated 4 does not extend the stated series. Predict the intended pattern, then inspect both the selection and the generated values.
CA-Q011: Deleting the entire row removes that record and shifts the lower rows together, preserving their within-row field relationships. Clearing contents leaves the row in place. Hiding changes visibility without removing the row. Deleting or clearing only one cell does not express the requested whole-record operation and can leave an incomplete or misaligned table.
CA-Q012: Undo can reverse the unintended fill while that operation is still reversible. Then inspect the destination before repeating it. Saving first does not restore overwritten contents; clearing the destination cannot reconstruct the previous values. Number formatting controls display and has no mechanism for recovering overwritten data. Recovery and prevention are separate steps.
CA-Q013: In $B$2, the dollar signs fix both the column B and row 2 during copying. B2 lets both coordinates move; $B2 fixes only the column, and B$2 fixes only the row. Read each coordinate separately. A dollar sign does not freeze the stored value or prevent the referenced input from changing.
CA-Q014: The colon selects the inclusive range B2, B3, B4 and B5. It therefore includes four cells rather than only the endpoints. Division uses /, and text joining uses &. Knowing the range endpoints is necessary before trusting an aggregate such as SUM, because the function operates on the selected inputs.
CA-Q015: A formula in D3 that uses D3 as its input depends on its own output: a circular reference. Fixing coordinates with dollar signs changes copying behavior, not that dependency. A normal reference to another worksheet is not inherently circular. Investigate the intended inputs instead of replacing the displayed result with an unexplained constant.
CA-Q016: Division is evaluated before addition: 27/3=9, then 6+9=15. The result 11 would follow from the different expression =(6+27)/3. A formula can be syntactically valid while expressing the wrong grouping. Use parentheses to make the intended mathematical relationship explicit rather than relying on the appearance of the typed expression.
CA-Q017: Moving the formula one row down changes relative B2 to B3 while absolute $F$1 remains fixed. Keeping B2 would reuse the previous row's quantity; changing F1 to F2 would move the shared parameter. A change to columns would describe a different copy direction. Inspect the copied formula, not just a plausible result.
CA-Q018: The dollar sign fixes column B, while row 2 is relative and becomes row 3 after moving down. The result is $B3. $C3 incorrectly moves the fixed column; $B2 incorrectly fixes the row; C$2 fixes the wrong component. Mixed references are easiest to predict by treating column and row independently.
CA-Q019: SUM adds the supplied numeric arguments or referenced values. MOD asks for a remainder, SQRT a square root and ABS a magnitude without sign; those functions can accept numbers while answering different questions. Start from the required meaning, such as total items, rather than choosing a function only because its input types fit.
CA-Q020: NOW() requests the current date and time when recalculation occurs. TODAY() is date-only; DATE constructs the supplied year/month/day, and TIME constructs a time from specified arguments. Formatting a NOW value to show only a date does not prove the time portion is absent. The source's contradictory TODAY wording remains flagged, with its candidate item withheld.
CA-Q021: DATE takes year, month and day in that order. A local date display or an ambiguous typed string may put those components in another visual order, but that does not change function syntax. Explicitly identifying the three arguments separates construction of the value from its display and avoids reversing the intended month and day.
CA-Q022: Three whole groups of five account for 15 of the 17 items, leaving 17−15=2. MOD returns that remainder, not the whole-group count 3 or the ordinary quotient 3.4. Five is the divisor. State whether the question asks for groups, a ratio or leftovers before selecting the calculation.
CA-Q023: SQRT(81) returns the nonnegative square root, 9, because 9*9=81. Squaring 81 produces 6561 and is the reverse kind of operation; dividing 81 by two gives 40.5 and does not find a square root. Distinguish a function's specified output from the two solutions of the separate equation x²=81.
CA-Q024: A deliberately stored event date preserves the chosen occurrence rather than following the current clock. TODAY and NOW can change on recalculation; they are not automatically permanent timestamps. A date format controls how an existing value appears and cannot supply a missing event date. Check both the stored input and the intended record meaning.
CA-Q025: COUNT counts numeric entries in the referenced range. COUNTA includes nonempty text as well, so it answers a different completeness question. A nonempty COUNTIF criterion does not restrict the count to numeric measurements, and SUM returns a total rather than a number of observations. Missing or pending measurements should not silently be treated as zeros.
CA-Q026: The median is the middle ordered value, or the mean of the two middle values when the numeric dataset has even size. The arithmetic mean uses all values and the mode concerns frequency; neither definition is based on the central ordered position. MAX identifies the largest value. For 2, 4, 9, the median is 4 and the mean is 5.
CA-Q027: The lecturer's legacy STDEV function estimates spread using a sample interpretation, while STDEVP concerns a whole population. Select that interpretation from the question or study design rather than from which button is convenient. Both concern variability, not just the mean or a count of nonempty cells. Selecting every available row does not by itself establish population status.
CA-Q028: The total is 2+4+9=15 and the number of observations is 3, giving the arithmetic mean 15/3=5. Four is the median, 15 the sum and 3 the count. These distractors are useful quantities but answer different questions. Name the statistic before calculating so that a correct intermediate result is not mistaken for the requested result.
CA-Q029: COUNT includes the two numeric entries, 10 and 12. COUNTA additionally includes the nonempty text pending, giving 3; neither counts the genuinely empty cell here. Pending is evidence of an entry, not a numeric observation. Replacing an empty cell with a space would change its contents, which is why genuine emptiness matters to this comparison.
CA-Q030: Evaluate the criterion for each value: 35 fails, each 40 qualifies, and 55 qualifies, so the count is 3. The >= operator includes equality; >40 would count only 55. Counting all four ignores the criterion, while counting two misses a qualifying entry. This calculation establishes operator behavior without deciding an official academic pass boundary.
CA-Q031: The ampersand joins text fragments, as in ="HB"&1 producing HB1. The caret denotes exponentiation, + is arithmetic addition and <> compares for inequality. Joining an identifier's characters is not equivalent to adding measured quantities. Inspect the intended result type before choosing an operator, especially for labels that contain digits.
CA-Q032: AND is true only when every supplied condition is true. OR permits at least one true condition, including the case where all are true. Therefore exactly one true condition is insufficient for AND when another condition is false. Trace each individual comparison first; then apply the combining rule rather than guessing from the original numbers.
CA-Q033: nper is the number of periods, such as 60 monthly periods in five years. Rate must use that same period basis. The periodic interest rate, present value and payment amount are different arguments; their numerical acceptability does not make them interchangeable. Write units beside inputs before entering a financial function.
CA-Q034: At B2=50 the comparison B2>=50 is true, so IF returns its true-branch text, Review complete. The false-branch label would apply below 50; the formula does not return the tested number or merely the comparison's Boolean result. Changing >= to > would change this boundary case. Fifty is an exercise threshold, not an institutional rule.
CA-Q035: The first comparison, 10>16, is false; the second, 20>10, is true. OR requires at least one true condition, so the result is TRUE. AND would be false for the same pair. The values 10 and 16 are inputs to comparisons, not outputs of this OR expression. Separate input values, truth values and final output.
CA-Q036: Monthly periods require both a monthly rate and a monthly count. Under the stated nominal-rate assumption, rate=12%/12=1% per month and nper=5*12=60 months. Twelve percent with 60 treats the annual figure as monthly; nper=5 with a monthly rate models five months. This does not establish payment timing, cash-flow signs or an official loan policy.
CA-Q037: A number format normally changes displayed appearance while calculations continue to use the stored numeric value. It does not rewrite formula references or change how many records exist. For example, 0.25 may display as 25% without becoming the stored number 25. Inspect the formula bar when display and calculation appear inconsistent.
CA-Q038: Save As lets you choose another file name, location or format. Ordinary Save usually updates the current destination. Format Painter copies formatting, and renaming a worksheet changes a tab inside the workbook rather than its file destination. Reopening the intended saved copy is a useful check that the file-level operation matched your purpose.
CA-Q039: A print area identifies the worksheet range intended for printed output. Cells outside it still exist in the workbook. Converting data to a chart and restricting permitted cell edits are separate operations. A correct print-area selection also does not guarantee readable scaling or repeated headings, so inspect Preview after setting it.
CA-Q040: Percentage display expresses the stored fraction relative to one: 0.25*100=25%, while the stored value stays 0.25. Entering 25 before applying that format would display 2500%, not repair the input. The percent symbol and scaling communicate a representation, so distinguish a display adjustment from changing the number used in formulas.
CA-Q041: Wrap Text permits a cell's long heading to occupy multiple lines within its available width. Check row height as well so the lines remain visible. Percentage formatting changes numeric display, sorting changes order, and merging unrelated records damages the table structure rather than addressing line wrapping. Choose an appearance operation that preserves the data's meaning.
CA-Q042: Print Preview reveals the selected output at its page size. Orientation and scaling can alter how the wide table fits; forcing one page may sacrifice readability. A tab colour, workbook name or copy count does not solve that layout problem. Inspect all pages and accept extra pages when needed rather than treating the smallest page count as success.
CA-Q043: A data series is a collection of related plotted values, such as department counts. Category labels identify the groups, while a chart title describes the chart and the plotting boundary frames it. None alone is the numeric series. Trace a visible point or bar to its source cell to check that the intended measurements were selected.
CA-Q044: An XY scatter chart places paired observations using numeric x and numeric y values, preserving unequal x intervals. A line chart using equally spaced categories does not represent those intervals in the same way. Pie and doughnut charts represent parts of a whole. Choose from the relationship between variables rather than simply from the chart's appearance.
CA-Q045: A single meaningful total divided into a few parts suits a pie chart's part-to-whole display. Paired numeric variables, several unrelated series or values without a coherent whole do not fit that interpretation. Check that the labels and selected series describe actual contributions; the ability to create slices is not evidence that a part-to-whole question is appropriate.
CA-Q046: A column chart is a useful starting point for comparing totals among distinct departments. The department names are categories, not measured numeric x values. A chronological line implies a sequence absent from the question, and unrelated pie series lack a single shared whole. Verify labels and selected values after choosing the chart.
CA-Q047: The x intervals are 2 days and 7 days, so numeric spacing carries information. An XY scatter chart can preserve those distances. A categorical line chart may space the labels equally, changing the visual interpretation. Pie and doughnut displays concern parts of a whole rather than the relationship between measurement day and count.
CA-Q048: A source-linked chart depends on its selected cells and series. Inspect the edited values, range and labels first to understand the new display. Font size, border colour and file name can change appearance or identification but do not establish which measurements are plotted. Interpret the result only after checking the dependency on the source data.
CA-Q049: A row normally holds the related fields for one record, such as an ID, group and count. Columns identify shared fields across records. Treating a row as an unrelated heading or worksheet confuses the table's structure. This distinction matters when sorting: the fields of one record must move together to preserve their associations.
CA-Q050: Sorting arranges records by specified fields and directions. Filtering instead limits which qualifying records are displayed. Neither operation inherently converts text to numbers or deletes low values. Inspect the complete selected table before sorting so that a correctly ordered count column does not become detached from its record identifiers.
CA-Q051: Filtering changes visibility according to criteria; it does not inherently replace stored values, delete excluded records or sort everything. Clearing a filter can reveal excluded rows again. If a record seems missing, inspect active criteria before entering a duplicate. A filtered display is a selected view of the underlying records, not proof that other records ceased to exist.
CA-Q052: Sort the complete table by its count field so every record's ID and other fields move with the count. Sorting either column independently can create false associations even while the selected column appears ordered. Sorting only the heading does not order the records. Check a known ID/count pair afterwards as a simple integrity check.
CA-Q053: The inclusive >=40 criterion retains both records at 40 and the record at 55, for three visible records. The 35 record is hidden rather than deleted. A count of one would correspond to >40 in this dataset. This distinction concerns comparison operators and does not establish whether 40 is officially a passing mark.
CA-Q054: The primary Group field brings group members together; the secondary Count descending orders records within each group. Count as the sole primary field mixes groups by size. Sorting the group column separately breaks records, while filtering out lower counts changes visibility rather than defining the requested within-group order. Select the complete record range.
CA-Q055: A slide layout defines where content placeholders are arranged. A theme coordinates fonts/colours/effects, slide order defines sequence, and transition timing governs changes between slides. Layout therefore concerns arrangement, not whether the inserted teaching material is correct. Choose a layout that serves the intended content, then inspect the content independently.
CA-Q056: A theme coordinates colours, fonts and effects across the presentation. Placeholder arrangement belongs to a layout; revealing an object belongs to animation; rearranging slide titles concerns sequence. A coordinated theme can improve consistency without correcting a faulty explanation or misplaced object. Visual consistency and academic correctness need separate checks.
CA-Q057: The .pptx format preserves a normal editable PowerPoint presentation with its slide objects. PDF is a fixed-layout output, JPG an image format and CSV a text table format; they do not preserve the same complete editing workflow. Retain the editable deck when exporting a viewing or printing copy for someone else.
CA-Q058: Title and Content supplies both the title and main content placeholders requested. Blank deliberately supplies neither, and title-only lacks the main content area. Choosing only a colour palette concerns theme appearance rather than the placeholder arrangement. A suitable starting layout still needs appropriate content and inspection after editing.
CA-Q059: Applying a theme addresses coordinated font and colour choices. Transitions act between slides, animations act on slide objects and reordering changes sequence, so those alternatives do not directly provide the requested coordinated scheme. Inspect all slides after applying the theme; consistency does not guarantee that each slide remains readable or correctly arranged.
CA-Q060: Retain the editable .pptx for later revision of slide objects and content. An image, printed handout or PDF can communicate an output view but does not preserve the same normal editing workflow. Keeping the source deck and an appropriate output copy serves different needs. Reopen the saved presentation before relying on it for collaboration.
CA-Q061: Grouping lets selected related objects move as a unit while retaining their relationship. Alignment instead places edges or centres relative to a reference, and stacking controls which overlapping object covers another. Grouping does not convert the objects into slides or automatically validate their content. Choose it when coordinated movement is the actual requirement.
CA-Q062: SmartArt supplies structured diagram layouts for relationships or processes. A transition controls a between-slide change, a worksheet formula calculates data and a print margin concerns page output. The diagram structure still needs a relationship that makes sense; selecting an attractive SmartArt arrangement does not establish a correct causal explanation.
CA-Q063: Send Backward moves the selected object one step toward the back of the stack. Send to Back moves it behind the whole stack; forward/front operations go the other direction. The distinction matters when several objects overlap. Inspect what covers what rather than assuming a single backward step always makes a label visible.
CA-Q064: Stacking order determines which overlapping object is drawn over another. A label hidden by a picture may need a front/back adjustment, followed by a visibility check. Border colour changes the picture outline; transition duration and file name do not change that overlap. Diagnose object relationships before altering unrelated presentation settings.
CA-Q065: Align Selected Objects makes the objects the alignment reference, and Align Top matches their top edges. Align to Slide uses the slide boundary instead. Align Bottom matches a different edge, while Send to Back changes overlap rather than edge alignment. Read both the reference and operation before applying an alignment command.
CA-Q066: Actual Slide Show playback on the delivery computer tests more of the needed workflow than a static icon or thumbnail. An object can be inserted while its media, sound or timing still fails at delivery. A border colour supplies no playback evidence. Target-version media acceptance remains an unexecuted practical check in this environment.
CA-Q067: Normal view supports creating and editing slide contents. Slide Sorter emphasizes thumbnails and sequence, Slide Show presents the audience view, and Print Preview exposes page output. Their purposes differ even though each displays a representation of the deck. Pick the view that reveals the operation you need to inspect.
CA-Q068: A transition governs movement between slides; an animation affects objects or text within a slide. Reordering thumbnails changes slide sequence, and a theme changes coordinated appearance. Neither is a synonym for both effects. Locate the level where the problem occurs—within a slide or between slides—before choosing the feature.
CA-Q069: Escape is the source-described command for ending a running Slide Show. Enter, Page Down and Right Arrow are associated with advancing through presentation content rather than the standard exit action. Exiting a show is different from closing or deleting the saved deck. This source-based answer does not mark the pending Office keyboard scenario as executed.
CA-Q070: Slide Sorter exposes many slide thumbnails for reviewing and changing their sequence. Full-screen Slide Show is for delivery, editing one text box in Normal view is a different task, and Print Preview concerns page output. After reordering, check whether the explanation still has a sensible beginning, progression and recap.
CA-Q071: Revealing three points one at a time on the same slide is an object/text animation task. A transition concerns movement to another slide. A theme changes coordinated appearance, and a new layout alone does not establish effect timing or order. Inspect the animation sequence rather than rearranging unrelated whole slides.
CA-Q072: Print Preview and the selected output/range let you check which pages or handouts will be printed and whether they are readable. Transition duration concerns slide delivery, the first title does not identify every output page, and editing zoom is not print layout. Check the actual output settings rather than an unrelated on-screen property.
CA-Q073: The source describes direct custom-list entries made from text or text mixed with numbers, such as ordered labels. It separately describes preparing numeric-only items as text in worksheet cells. A custom list is not restricted to formulas or cell references, and its defining feature is the intended ordered sequence, not that every item is a date.
CA-Q074: Import reads entries from the selected worksheet range, which is the source already available in this scenario. NEW LIST begins manually typed entry, Add stores the typed entries and Delete removes a selected list. Check the imported range and order: using the appropriate button does not prove the cells chosen were correct.
CA-Q075: NEW LIST selects the workflow for typing a new ordered list. After completing the entries, Add stores them. Import instead reads an existing worksheet range, and Delete removes a list. Distinguish beginning creation from completing it; the two stages explain why NEW LIST and Add are related but not interchangeable answers.
CA-Q076: Add stores the entries already typed in List entries. NEW LIST starts that typing workflow but is not its final storage action. Import is appropriate for entries in worksheet cells, and Delete removes rather than saves. Inspect the resulting stored sequence before using it to fill a destination range.
CA-Q077: Descriptive names expose input roles, making a formula such as =Unit_Price*Quantity easier to interpret than unexplained coordinates. They do not guarantee correct references or calculations. Sorting rows and replacing worksheet tabs are unrelated. A readable formula still requires checking each name's definition and the meaning of the inputs it points to.
CA-Q078: _Price begins with an underscore, meeting the lecturer's stated initial-character rule. The other choices begin with a hyphen, space or digit and do not meet that stated rule. This item assesses the source's basic example rather than an exhaustive specification of every valid Excel name, scope or reference behavior.
CA-Q079: The Name Box is at the left end of the formula bar and can show an active address or defined name. Sheet tabs identify worksheets, and the status bar and grid serve different purposes. Its location helps distinguish selecting or defining a range name from renaming a sheet or changing a cell's displayed contents.
CA-Q080: Name Manager provides a place to inspect and manage several defined names, including their referenced ranges. Print Preview and Page Layout concern output/layout; chart tools concern plotted data. Neither those commands nor readable names themselves verify the inputs. Inspect Refers To when investigating a named formula that produces an unexpected result.
CA-Q081: The space in CSM 1 requires the sheet name to be enclosed in single quotes, with ! separating it from A10: 'CSM 1'!A10. A colon denotes a range, not that separator, and reversing sheet/address order changes the reference structure. This is the reference portion; a formula using it starts with =.
CA-Q082: An exclamation mark separates the worksheet name from its cell or range, as in Sheet2!A1. A colon specifies a range, dollar signs fix reference coordinates during copying and an ampersand joins text. Those symbols address different relationships, so choosing one because it also appears in formulas is insufficient.
CA-Q083: Sheet1:Sheet4 specifies the inclusive worksheet span from the first endpoint tab to the last, not just the two endpoint sheets. !D1 then selects the cell within that span. Dollar signs, not this sheet colon, express absolute coordinates. Inspect tab order because intermediate worksheets determine which sources a span includes.
CA-Q084: =SUM(Sheet1:Sheet4!D1:D10) combines a worksheet span with a within-sheet cell range. The first colon selects sheets, ! separates that part from the cells, and the second colon includes D1 through D10. The alternatives scramble those roles. In the worked four-sheet example, four individual totals of 55 give the cross-sheet total 220.
CA-Q085: VLOOKUP matches the source-described direction: search down the table's first column and return a related value across the matching row. HLOOKUP searches the top row instead, ROWS counts a range's rows and MATCH concerns a position. Direction identifies the appropriate family here; detailed arguments and match behavior remain separate review work.
CA-Q086: HLOOKUP searches across the top row and returns a value from a specified row in the matching column. COLUMN identifies a position, INDEX selects a value through an index and OFFSET concerns a reference displacement. The table orientation distinguishes this from a first-column search; it does not establish a full argument specification.
CA-Q087: MATCH reports the target's position relative to the start of a selected range. In the labelled technical clarification, MATCH(6,B2:B3,0) returns 2 for values 4 and 6, not the matched value 6 or worksheet row 3. TRANSPOSE changes orientation; INDIRECT and LOOKUP have other reference/search roles. The lecturer's glossary alone is terse, so the more specific interpretation remains separately documented.
CA-Q088: TRANSPOSE exchanges row and column orientation. ROW and COLUMN identify positions, while CHOOSE selects using an index; none means reorienting the entire arrangement. A horizontal list becoming vertical illustrates the task without requiring a search for a key. Detailed target-version entry behavior is not certified by this glossary question.
CA-Q089: The master worksheet is the summary destination for consolidated results. Hidden or protected describes visibility or edit restrictions; neither identifies the aggregation role, and a chart worksheet is a different destination type. Name the sources, operation and destination separately before executing consolidation. Actual 542-page PDF p.305 supports this terminology.
CA-Q090: The destination range is where combined results appear; source ranges supply the contributing inputs. A legend concerns a chart, and a protection list concerns permitted operations. Mixing the source and output roles can overwrite data or summarize the wrong cells even if the chosen aggregation function is correct. Actual lecturer PDF p.306 is the reconciled citation.
CA-Q091: Links can let the consolidated output reflect subsequent source changes, whereas a fixed summary is a snapshot. Updating inputs does not imply deletion, text conversion or removal of protection. Inspect the chosen link option and source references rather than assuming every summary stays live. Actual lecturer PDF p.309 supports the fixed/linked distinction.
CA-Q092: The intended SUM is 12+15+23=50. Twenty-three is only one input; 38 omits 12, and 45 is not the stated sum. A plausible-looking number is not sufficient: confirm all intended sources were included exactly once and represent the same category. This fictional arithmetic does not select an official payroll rule.
CA-Q093: A horizontal break after the intended row uses the active cell below that boundary in the source-described operation. Selecting above places attention on the wrong boundary; a row heading or last worksheet column does not define the requested split. Pagination changes the output boundary rather than moving source values. The target Excel insertion action remains unexecuted.
CA-Q094: Manual breaks influence pagination by overriding automatic breaks and causing their positions to adjust. They do not delete cells or permanently insert blank records, and a print area still answers which cells should be output. Reinspect Preview after changing breaks or scaling; a chosen boundary alone does not establish readable output on every page.
CA-Q095: The source assigns print area, print titles and page order to the Sheet tab. Page concerns settings such as orientation/size, Margins concerns spacing and Header/Footer concerns repeated information outside the worksheet body. These controls address related but distinct output needs. The answer identifies source wording rather than certifying one universal dialog layout.
CA-Q096: A header places repeated information above the printed worksheet body without adding false data records. Renaming a tab or changing a chart legend does not request page-top identification. Inserting data rows on every page confuses source observations with output layout. Distinguish repeated column headings, which use print titles, from a page title/number in the header.
CA-Q097: Both placeholders and text boxes can use the same text-formatting commands according to the source. They remain distinct containers with different placement roles. A text box does not need conversion to a table, and formatting one does not inherently change every slide. Inspect the actual selection when choosing which text to format.
CA-Q098: Center text alignment acts within the selected text container. It does not move the box to the slide centre or align every slide object. If the whole box is misplaced, adjust its position or object alignment instead. A correctly centred line inside a left-positioned box can therefore still appear near the slide edge.
CA-Q099: Background styles are fill variations based on theme colours, so changing the theme can change the available variations. The file name and slide count do not define those colours, and a theme change does not inherently delete every picture. Inspect the coordinated appearance across slides without confusing it with content or object removal.
CA-Q100: A numbered list explicitly communicates an ordered procedure. Bullets and picture bullets mark items without inherently numbering their sequence; unnumbered paragraphs provide no such sequence markers. The source's actual 542-page reference is p.454, not the package's p.453. Numbering is useful only when the stated order itself is meaningful and correct.
CA-Q101: Start at controls the first number in the source-described numbering dialog. Font size and line spacing affect text appearance; the slide number identifies a slide rather than the list's first item. Use the field appropriate to the content hierarchy. A continued list beginning at 4 does not require changing the slide order.
CA-Q102: Justify aligns text with both container margins. Align Left and Align Right constrain one side, while Center positions each line around the centre. Text alignment concerns the text inside its box, not moving the whole box across the slide. Choose the setting based on the intended line arrangement rather than the container's location.
CA-Q103: The source names Tab for moving the insertion point between table cells, with mouse/arrow navigation also discussed. Escape, Caps Lock and Print Screen serve different purposes and do not express that table-navigation action. Where the insertion point lies matters before inserting a row or column. The target PowerPoint keyboard operation has not been executed here.
CA-Q104: The source places Insert Above in contextual Table Tools → Layout, relative to the selected row. Borders changes table lines, indent changes paragraph layout and drawing a table does not directly express adding that adjacent row. The reconciled actual-PDF citation is p.460, corresponding to package p.459; the target-version dialog still needs execution.
CA-Q105: Insert Right adds a column to the right of the current table selection. Insert Above and Insert Below add rows instead, while Merge Cells combines existing cells rather than adding a column. Identify whether the requested structural change concerns rows or columns before choosing a directional command. A transition cannot alter table structure.
CA-Q106: Weight changes the border line's width while leaving the selected colour unchanged. Volume concerns audio, transition duration concerns between-slide effects and paragraph spacing concerns text. The scenario already identifies colour as correct, so changing colour again does not address thickness. Separate picture content, object size and border appearance when troubleshooting.
CA-Q107: The source warns that a side sizing handle can change a picture's proportions. Moving the whole object changes location, and changing border colour or slide order does not itself stretch the picture. Inspect the resulting shape after resizing rather than assuming the original image was altered. Target-version aspect-ratio controls still need separate checking.
CA-Q108: Volume directly addresses playback loudness. Loop Until Stopped concerns repetition, Hide During Show concerns icon visibility and Trim Audio selects a portion of the media. None of those is a substitute for adjusting loudness. Actual lecturer PDF p.511 is the reconciled source page; real PowerPoint playback on the delivery computer remains unexecuted.
